claim: In eukaryotes, exposure to hypertonic conditions activates a MAPK (Hog1 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and ortholog p38 in human cells).
source: In eukaryotes, exposure to hypertonic conditions activates a MAPK (Hog1 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and ortholog p38 in human cells).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MAPK activation in response to hypertonic stress across eukaryotes.

claim: In yeast, intracellular glycerol accumulates to counterbalance the high external osmolarity.
source: In yeast, intracellular glycerol accumulates to counterbalance the high external osmolarity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast osmotic stress response.

claim: Hog1 action impedes the function of the aquaglyceroporin Fps1, in part, by displacing channel co-activators (Rgc1/2).
source: To prevent glycerol efflux, Hog1 action impedes the function of the aquaglyceroporin Fps1, in part, by displacing channel co-activators (Rgc1/2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hog1 regulation of Fps1.

claim: Fps1 closes upon hyperosmotic shock even in hog1∆ cells.
source: However, Fps1 closes upon hyperosmotic shock even in hog1∆ cells, indicating another mechanism to prevent Fps1-mediated glycerol efflux.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature and indicates the existence of a Hog1-independent mechanism.

claim: Fps1 was identified as a target of TORC2-dependent protein kinase Ypk1 in a prior proteome-wide screen.
source: In our prior proteome-wide screen, Fps1 was identified as a target of TORC2-dependent protein kinase Ypk1 (Muir et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Muir et al., 2014).

claim: Fps1 is an authentic Ypk1 substrate.
source: We show here that Fps1 is an authentic Ypk1 substrate and that the open channel state of Fps1 requires phosphorylation by Ypk1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including phosphorylation assays and mobility shift experiments.

claim: The open channel state of Fps1 requires phosphorylation by Ypk1.
source: We show here that Fps1 is an authentic Ypk1 substrate and that the open channel state of Fps1 requires phosphorylation by Ypk1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Fps13A mutant (lacking Ypk1 phosphorylation sites) behaves like a closed channel.

claim: Hyperosmotic conditions block TORC2-dependent Ypk1-mediated Fps1 phosphorylation.
source: Moreover, hyperosmotic conditions block TORC2-dependent Ypk1-mediated Fps1 phosphorylation, causing channel closure, glycerol accumulation, and enhanced survival under hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of Fps1 phosphorylation upon hyperosmotic shock.

claim: Hyperosmotic conditions cause channel closure of Fps1.
source: Moreover, hyperosmotic conditions block TORC2-dependent Ypk1-mediated Fps1 phosphorylation, causing channel closure, glycerol accumulation, and enhanced survival under hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation and the arsenite resistance phenotype.

claim: Hyperosmotic conditions cause glycerol accumulation.
source: Moreover, hyperosmotic conditions block TORC2-dependent Ypk1-mediated Fps1 phosphorylation, causing channel closure, glycerol accumulation, and enhanced survival under hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased intracellular glycerol in Fps13A cells.

claim: Hyperosmotic conditions cause enhanced survival under hyperosmotic stress.
source: Moreover, hyperosmotic conditions block TORC2-dependent Ypk1-mediated Fps1 phosphorylation, causing channel closure, glycerol accumulation, and enhanced survival under hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Fps13A hog1Δ cells survive better than hog1Δ cells under hyperosmotic stress.

claim: The events of channel closure, glycerol accumulation, and enhanced survival are all Hog1-independent.
source: These events are all Hog1-independent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Fps13A confers arsenite resistance and survival benefits even in hog1Δ cells.

claim: TORC2-dependent signaling responds to sphingolipid depletion.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, target of rapamycin (TOR) Complex 2 (TORC2)-dependent signaling responds to multiple plasma membrane-perturbing stresses, including sphingolipid depletion (Roelants et al., 2010, 2011), heat shock (Sun et al., 2012), and both hypotonic (Berchtold et al., 2012) and hypertonic (Lee et al., 2012) conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TORC2-dependent signaling responds to heat shock.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, target of rapamycin (TOR) Complex 2 (TORC2)-dependent signaling responds to multiple plasma membrane-perturbing stresses, including sphingolipid depletion (Roelants et al., 2010, 2011), heat shock (Sun et al., 2012), and both hypotonic (Berchtold et al., 2012) and hypertonic (Lee et al., 2012) conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: TORC2-dependent signaling responds to hypotonic conditions.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, target of rapamycin (TOR) Complex 2 (TORC2)-dependent signaling responds to multiple plasma membrane-perturbing stresses, including sphingolipid depletion (Roelants et al., 2010, 2011), heat shock (Sun et al., 2012), and both hypotonic (Berchtold et al., 2012) and hypertonic (Lee et al., 2012) conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Berchtold et al., 2012.

claim: TORC2-dependent signaling responds to hypertonic conditions.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, target of rapamycin (TOR) Complex 2 (TORC2)-dependent signaling responds to multiple plasma membrane-perturbing stresses, including sphingolipid depletion (Roelants et al., 2010, 2011), heat shock (Sun et al., 2012), and both hypotonic (Berchtold et al., 2012) and hypertonic (Lee et al., 2012) conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: The essential downstream effector of TORC2 is the protein kinase Ypk1 (and its paralog Ypk2).
source: The essential downstream effector of TORC2 is the protein kinase Ypk1 (and its paralog Ypk2) (Casamayor et al., 1999; Roelants et al., 2002, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A genome-wide screen was performed to discern previously unidentified Ypk1 substrates.
source: To understand how TORC2-Ypk1 signaling elicits cellular responses, we performed a genome-wide screen to discern previously unidentified Ypk1 substrates and thereby discovered that ceramide synthase activity is stimulated by TORC2-Ypk1 (Muir et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Ceramide synthase activity is stimulated by TORC2-Ypk1.
source: To understand how TORC2-Ypk1 signaling elicits cellular responses, we performed a genome-wide screen to discern previously unidentified Ypk1 substrates and thereby discovered that ceramide synthase activity is stimulated by TORC2-Ypk1 (Muir et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Muir et al., 2014.

claim: The screen pinpointed aquaglyceroporin Fps1 as a potential Ypk1 target.
source: Among other potential targets, our screen pinpointed two proteins involved in glycerol metabolism, aquaglyceroporin Fps1 (Luyten et al., 1995) and Gpt2/Gat1, an enzyme that converts glycerol-3P to phosphatidic acid (Zheng and Zou, 2001), a precursor to other phospholipids and triacylglycerol (Henry et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' screen results.

claim: The screen pinpointed Gpt2/Gat1 as a potential Ypk1 target.
source: Among other potential targets, our screen pinpointed two proteins involved in glycerol metabolism, aquaglyceroporin Fps1 (Luyten et al., 1995) and Gpt2/Gat1, an enzyme that converts glycerol-3P to phosphatidic acid (Zheng and Zou, 2001), a precursor to other phospholipids and triacylglycerol (Henry et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' screen results.

claim: Gpt2/Gat1 is an enzyme that converts glycerol-3P to phosphatidic acid.
source: Among other potential targets, our screen pinpointed two proteins involved in glycerol metabolism, aquaglyceroporin Fps1 (Luyten et al., 1995) and Gpt2/Gat1, an enzyme that converts glycerol-3P to phosphatidic acid (Zheng and Zou, 2001), a precursor to other phospholipids and triacylglycerol (Henry et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zheng and Zou, 2001.

claim: Phosphatidic acid is a precursor to other phospholipids and triacylglycerol.
source: Among other potential targets, our screen pinpointed two proteins involved in glycerol metabolism, aquaglyceroporin Fps1 (Luyten et al., 1995) and Gpt2/Gat1, an enzyme that converts glycerol-3P to phosphatidic acid (Zheng and Zou, 2001), a precursor to other phospholipids and triacylglycerol (Henry et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Henry et al., 2012.

claim: Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation inhibits Gpd1, which generates glycerol-3P.
source: Both candidates warranted further investigation because, as we showed, Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation inhibits another enzyme in glycerol metabolism, Gpd1, which generates glycerol-3P (Lee et al., 2012), and GPD1 expression is highly induced by hyperosmotic stress (Albertyn et al., 1994b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: GPD1 expression is highly induced by hyperosmotic stress.
source: Both candidates warranted further investigation because, as we showed, Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation inhibits another enzyme in glycerol metabolism, Gpd1, which generates glycerol-3P (Lee et al., 2012), and GPD1 expression is highly induced by hyperosmotic stress (Albertyn et al., 1994b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Albertyn et al., 1994b.

claim: Accumulation of intercellular glycerol is essential for yeast cell survival under hyperosmotic conditions.
source: Second, accumulation of intercellular glycerol is essential for yeast cell survival under hyperosmotic conditions (Westfall et al., 2008; Saito and Posas, 2012; Hohmann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hyperosmotic conditions evoke pathways coupled to alternative osmosensors (Sln1 and Sho1) that activate MAPK Hog1.
source: Hyperosmotic conditions evoke two known signaling modalities. Pathways coupled to alternative osmosensors (Sln1 and Sho1) activate MAPK Hog1, which drives both transcription-independent and -dependent responses that markedly increase both production and intracellular retention of glycerol (Westfall et al., 2008; Saito and Posas, 2012; Hohmann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hog1 drives both transcription-independent and -dependent responses that markedly increase both production and intracellular retention of glycerol.
source: Pathways coupled to alternative osmosensors (Sln1 and Sho1) activate MAPK Hog1, which drives both transcription-independent and -dependent responses that markedly increase both production and intracellular retention of glycerol (Westfall et al., 2008; Saito and Posas, 2012; Hohmann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hyperosmotic shock increases cytosolic [Ca2+] thereby activating calcineurin (CN).
source: Hyperosmotic shock also increases cytosolic [Ca2+] thereby activating calcineurin (CN) (Denis and Cyert, 2002), promoting processes that stimulate retrieval of excess plasma membrane (Guiney et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Denis and Cyert, 2002.

claim: Calcineurin activation promotes processes that stimulate retrieval of excess plasma membrane.
source: Hyperosmotic shock also increases cytosolic [Ca2+] thereby activating calcineurin (CN) (Denis and Cyert, 2002), promoting processes that stimulate retrieval of excess plasma membrane (Guiney et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guiney et al., 2015.

claim: Both CN-deficient and hog1∆ cells are quite sensitive to the ionic imbalances caused by high salt (e.g., 1 M NaCl).
source: Although both CN-deficient and hog1∆ cells are quite sensitive to the ionic imbalances caused by high salt (e.g., 1 M NaCl), hog1∆ cells are significantly more sensitive to hypertonic stress per se, such as a high concentration of an uncharged impermeant osmolyte (e.g., 1 M sorbitol).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast stress responses.

claim: hog1∆ cells are significantly more sensitive to hypertonic stress per se, such as a high concentration of an uncharged impermeant osmolyte (e.g., 1 M sorbitol).
source: Although both CN-deficient and hog1∆ cells are quite sensitive to the ionic imbalances caused by high salt (e.g., 1 M NaCl), hog1∆ cells are significantly more sensitive to hypertonic stress per se, such as a high concentration of an uncharged impermeant osmolyte (e.g., 1 M sorbitol).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast stress responses.

claim: Preventing glycerol efflux through the aquaglyceroporin Fps1 is essential for yeast to survive hyperosmolarity.
source: Although it is well documented that preventing glycerol efflux through the aquaglyceroporin Fps1 is essential for yeast to survive hyperosmolarity (Luyten et al., 1995; Tamás et al., 1999; Duskova et al., 2015), and that activated Hog1 can negatively regulate this channel by displacing the Fps1-activating proteins Rgc1/2 (Lee et al., 2013), Fps1 still closes in response to hyperosmotic shock in hog1∆ cells (Tamás et al., 1999; Babazadeh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activated Hog1 can negatively regulate Fps1 channel by displacing the Fps1-activating proteins Rgc1/2.
source: Although it is well documented that preventing glycerol efflux through the aquaglyceroporin Fps1 is essential for yeast to survive hyperosmolarity (Luyten et al., 1995; Tamás et al., 1999; Duskova et al., 2015), and that activated Hog1 can negatively regulate this channel by displacing the Fps1-activating proteins Rgc1/2 (Lee et al., 2013), Fps1 still closes in response to hyperosmotic shock in hog1∆ cells (Tamás et al., 1999; Babazadeh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Fps1 still closes in response to hyperosmotic shock in hog1∆ cells.
source: Although it is well documented that preventing glycerol efflux through the aquaglyceroporin Fps1 is essential for yeast to survive hyperosmolarity (Luyten et al., 1995; Tamás et al., 1999; Duskova et al., 2015), and that activated Hog1 can negatively regulate this channel by displacing the Fps1-activating proteins Rgc1/2 (Lee et al., 2013), Fps1 still closes in response to hyperosmotic shock in hog1∆ cells (Tamás et al., 1999; Babazadeh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tamás et al., 1999 and Babazadeh et al., 2014.

claim: The 743-residue enzyme Gpt2 contains one Ypk1 phospho-acceptor motif (646RSRSSSI652).
source: The 743-residue enzyme Gpt2 contains one Ypk1 phospho-acceptor motif (646RSRSSSI652).
evidence: This is a sequence analysis result from the manuscript.

claim: At Ypk1 phospho-acceptor sites, Ser residues just penultimate to the canonical one can be phosphorylated in a Ypk1-dependent manner.
source: At such sites, Ser residues just penultimate to the canonical one (in red) can be phosphorylated in a Ypk1-dependent manner (Roelants et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roelants et al., 2011.

claim: One or more of the three Ser residues (S649, S650, S651) in Gpt2 is phosphorylated in vivo.
source: One or more of these three Ser residues is phosphorylated in vivo because, compared to wild-type, Gpt23A exhibited a distinctly faster mobility upon SDS-PAGE, a hallmark of decreased phosphorylation (Figure 1A), just like wild-type Gpt2 treated with phosphatase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing mobility shift on SDS-PAGE and phosphatase treatment.

claim: Gpt2 phosphorylation does not appear to be dependent on Ypk1.
source: However, this phosphorylation did not appear to be dependent on Ypk1 because little change occurred in Gpt2 mobility when an analog-sensitive ypk1-as ypk2Δ strain was treated with the cognate inhibitor (3-MB-PP1) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in Gpt2 mobility upon Ypk1 inhibition.

claim: Three of four predicted Ypk1 sites in the 669-residue Fps1 channel (176RRRSRSR182, 180RSRATSN186, 565RARRTSD571) are phosphorylated in vivo.
source: In marked contrast, three of four predicted Ypk1 sites in the 669-residue Fps1 channel (176RRRSRSR182, 180RSRATSN186, 565RARRTSD571) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) are phosphorylated in vivo, as indicated by the effect of site-directed mutations to Ala on electrophoretic mobility (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and their phosphorylation requires Ypk1 activity, because, in inhibitor-treated ypk1-as ypk2Δ cells, the mobility of wild-type Fps1 was indistinguishable from that of Fps1(S181A S185A S570A) (Figure 1B), just like wild-type Fps1 treated with phosphatase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing mobility shifts upon site-directed mutagenesis and Ypk1 inhibition.

claim: Fps1 phosphorylation at the three sites requires Ypk1 activity.
source: In marked contrast, three of four predicted Ypk1 sites in the 669-residue Fps1 channel (176RRRSRSR182, 180RSRATSN186, 565RARRTSD571) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) are phosphorylated in vivo, as indicated by the effect of site-directed mutations to Ala on electrophoretic mobility (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and their phosphorylation requires Ypk1 activity, because, in inhibitor-treated ypk1-as ypk2Δ cells, the mobility of wild-type Fps1 was indistinguishable from that of Fps1(S181A S185A S570A) (Figure 1B), just like wild-type Fps1 treated with phosphatase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Ypk1 inhibition eliminates the mobility difference between wild-type and mutant Fps1.

claim: A C-terminal fragment of Fps1 containing Ser570 is phosphorylated by purified Ypk1 in vitro and solely at the Ypk1 site (S570).
source: Moreover, a C-terminal fragment of Fps1 containing Ser570, one of the apparent Ypk1 phosphorylation sites delineated in vivo, is phosphorylated by purified Ypk1 in vitro and solely at the Ypk1 site (S570) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data.

claim: Phosphorylation of the same sites in Fps1 in vivo is TORC2-dependent.
source: Furthermore, as for other Ypk1-dependent modifications (Muir et al., 2014), phosphorylation of these same sites in Fps1 in vivo was also TORC2-dependent, because treatment with a TORC2 inhibitor (NVP-BEZ235) (Kliegman et al., 2013) also reduced Fps1 phosphorylation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced Fps1 phosphorylation upon TORC2 inhibition.

claim: Ypk1 phosphorylation at T662 is eliminated when cells are subjected to hyperosmotic shock for 10 min.
source: We documented elsewhere using Phos-tag gel mobility shift that Ypk1 phosphorylation at T662, one of its well-characterized TORC2 sites, is eliminated when cells are subjected to hyperosmotic shock for 10 min (Lee et al., 2012), and the same effect is observed using a specific antibody (Niles et al., 2012) that monitors phosphorylation of Ypk1 at the same site (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2012 and experimental data using a phospho-specific antibody.

claim: Loss of TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation upon hyperosmotic shock occurs very rapidly (within 1 min) and persists for about 15 min.
source: Loss of TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation upon hyperosmotic shock occurs very rapidly (within 1 min) and persists for about 15 min (Figure 1D), but is transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing kinetics of Ypk1 dephosphorylation.

claim: Loss of TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation upon hyperosmotic shock is transient.
source: Loss of TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation upon hyperosmotic shock occurs very rapidly (within 1 min) and persists for about 15 min (Figure 1D), but is transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing recovery of Ypk1 phosphorylation over time.

claim: By 20 min after hyperosmotic shock, TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation is again detectable and is nearly back to the pre-stress level by 75 min.
source: By 20 min after hyperosmotic shock, TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation is again detectable and is nearly back to the pre-stress level by 75 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing time course of Ypk1 phosphorylation recovery.

claim: Rapid reduction in TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation under hypertonic stress was still observed in mutants lacking the Sho1- or Sln1-dependent pathways that converge on Hog1 or Hog1 itself.
source: Rapid reduction in TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation under hypertonic stress was still observed in mutants lacking the Sho1- or Sln1-dependent pathways that converge on Hog1 or Hog1 itself (Figure 1E) or CN (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Ypk1 dephosphorylation in various mutant backgrounds.

claim: Rapid reduction in TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation under hypertonic stress was still observed in mutants lacking CN.
source: Rapid reduction in TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation under hypertonic stress was still observed in mutants lacking the Sho1- or Sln1-dependent pathways that converge on Hog1 or Hog1 itself (Figure 1E) or CN (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Ypk1 dephosphorylation in CN-deficient cells.

claim: Loss of TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation upon hyperosmotic shock occurs independently of other known response pathways.
source: Thus, loss of TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation upon hyperosmotic shock occurs independently of other known response pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing Ypk1 dephosphorylation in mutants lacking Hog1 and CN pathways.

claim: Ypk1 phosphorylation of Fps1 is rapidly lost upon hyperosmotic shock.
source: As expected, Ypk1 phosphorylation of Fps1 is rapidly lost upon hyperosmotic shock (Figure 1G), yielding a species with mobility indistinguishable from Fps13A, remains low for at least 20 min, but returns by 75 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), mirroring the kinetics of loss and return of both TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A) and Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation of Gpd1 that we observed before (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Fps1 mobility shift upon hyperosmotic shock.

claim: Ypk1 phosphorylation of Fps1 remains low for at least 20 min after hyperosmotic shock, but returns by 75 min.
source: As expected, Ypk1 phosphorylation of Fps1 is rapidly lost upon hyperosmotic shock (Figure 1G), yielding a species with mobility indistinguishable from Fps13A, remains low for at least 20 min, but returns by 75 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), mirroring the kinetics of loss and return of both TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A) and Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation of Gpd1 that we observed before (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing time course of Fps1 phosphorylation.

claim: The kinetics of Fps1 phosphorylation loss and return mirror the kinetics of loss and return of TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation.
source: As expected, Ypk1 phosphorylation of Fps1 is rapidly lost upon hyperosmotic shock (Figure 1G), yielding a species with mobility indistinguishable from Fps13A, remains low for at least 20 min, but returns by 75 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), mirroring the kinetics of loss and return of both TORC2-mediated Ypk1 phosphorylation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A) and Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation of Gpd1 that we observed before (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the time courses of Fps1 and Ypk1 phosphorylation.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress dramatically down-modulates Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation of Fps1.
source: Thus, hyperosmotic stress dramatically down-modulates Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation of Fps1.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data on Fps1 phosphorylation kinetics.

claim: In its open state, the Fps1 channel permits entry of toxic metalloid, arsenite, which inhibits growth.
source: In its open state, the Fps1 channel permits entry of toxic metalloid, arsenite, which inhibits growth (Thorsen et al., 2006), whereas lack of Fps1 (fps1∆) or the lack of channel activators (rgc1∆ rgc2∆) (Beese et al., 2009) or an Fps1 mutant that cannot open because it cannot bind the activators (Fps1∆PHD) (Lee et al., 2013) are arsenite resistant.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thorsen et al., 2006.

claim: Lack of Fps1 (fps1∆) confers arsenite resistance.
source: In its open state, the Fps1 channel permits entry of toxic metalloid, arsenite, which inhibits growth (Thorsen et al., 2006), whereas lack of Fps1 (fps1∆) or the lack of channel activators (rgc1∆ rgc2∆) (Beese et al., 2009) or an Fps1 mutant that cannot open because it cannot bind the activators (Fps1∆PHD) (Lee et al., 2013) are arsenite resistant.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Fps1 function.

claim: Lack of channel activators (rgc1∆ rgc2∆) confers arsenite resistance.
source: In its open state, the Fps1 channel permits entry of toxic metalloid, arsenite, which inhibits growth (Thorsen et al., 2006), whereas lack of Fps1 (fps1∆) or the lack of channel activators (rgc1∆ rgc2∆) (Beese et al., 2009) or an Fps1 mutant that cannot open because it cannot bind the activators (Fps1∆PHD) (Lee et al., 2013) are arsenite resistant.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Beese et al., 2009.

claim: An Fps1 mutant that cannot open because it cannot bind the activators (Fps1∆PHD) confers arsenite resistance.
source: In its open state, the Fps1 channel permits entry of toxic metalloid, arsenite, which inhibits growth (Thorsen et al., 2006), whereas lack of Fps1 (fps1∆) or the lack of channel activators (rgc1∆ rgc2∆) (Beese et al., 2009) or an Fps1 mutant that cannot open because it cannot bind the activators (Fps1∆PHD) (Lee et al., 2013) are arsenite resistant.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Fps13A was at least as arsenite resistant as any other mutant that abrogates Fps1 function.
source: We found that Fps13A was at least as arsenite resistant as any other mutant that abrogates Fps1 function (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing arsenite resistance of Fps13A.

claim: Fps13A acts like a closed channel.
source: Thus, Fps13A acts like a closed channel, suggesting that Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation promotes channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from the arsenite resistance phenotype of Fps13A.

claim: Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation promotes channel opening.
source: Thus, Fps13A acts like a closed channel, suggesting that Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation promotes channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Fps13A (lacking Ypk1 phosphorylation sites) acts like a closed channel.

claim: Loss of individual phosphorylation sites led to intermediate levels of arsenite resistance.
source: Loss of individual phosphorylation sites led to intermediate levels of arsenite resistance (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing arsenite resistance of single-site mutants.

claim: Modification at the Ypk1 sites contributes additively to channel opening.
source: Thus, modification at these sites contributes additively to channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from the intermediate arsenite resistance of single-site mutants.

claim: Intracellular glycerol is elevated in fps1∆ cells in the absence of hyperosmotic stress.
source: Others have shown that intracellular glycerol is elevated in fps1∆ cells in the absence of hyperosmotic stress (Tamás et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tamás et al., 1999.

claim: Fps13A mutant cells accumulated ∼twofold as much glycerol as otherwise isogenic FPS1+ strains in the absence of any osmotic perturbation.
source: Indeed, in the absence of any osmotic perturbation, Fps13A mutant cells accumulated ∼twofold as much glycerol as otherwise isogenic FPS1+ strains (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring intracellular glycerol levels.

claim: Loss of Ypk1 (and Ypk2) activity caused an increase in glycerol level compared to control cells.
source: Consistent with this result, we observed before that loss of Ypk1 (and Ypk2) activity caused an increase in glycerol level compared to control cells (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: The steady-state level and localization of Fps1 are unaffected by the presence or absence of Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation.
source: Consistent with Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation affecting Fps1 channel function per se, immunoblotting (Figure 2D) and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2E) showed that the steady-state level and localization of Fps1 are unaffected by the presence or absence of these modifications.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblotting and fluorescence microscopy.

claim: Fps1 can be negatively regulated by Hog1 via two mechanisms: Hog1 phosphorylation of Fps1 stimulates its internalization and degradation.
source: Fps1 can be negatively regulated by Hog1 via two mechanisms: Hog1 phosphorylation of Fps1 stimulates its internalization and degradation (Thorsen et al., 2006; Mollapour and Piper, 2007); Hog1 phosphorylation closes the channel by displacing bound Fps1 activators (Rgc1 and Rgc2) (Beese et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hog1 phosphorylation closes the Fps1 channel by displacing bound Fps1 activators (Rgc1 and Rgc2).
source: Fps1 can be negatively regulated by Hog1 via two mechanisms: Hog1 phosphorylation of Fps1 stimulates its internalization and degradation (Thorsen et al., 2006; Mollapour and Piper, 2007); Hog1 phosphorylation closes the channel by displacing bound Fps1 activators (Rgc1 and Rgc2) (Beese et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beese et al., 2009 and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Fps13A was still in the closed state in the total absence of Hog1 (hog1Δ).
source: We found, however, that Fps13A was still in the closed state, as judged by arsenite resistance, in the total absence of Hog1 (hog1Δ) (Figure 3A), or in an Fps1 mutant (Fps1IVAA) that cannot bind Hog1 or where the activator cannot be displaced from Fps1 by Hog1 phosphorylation (Rgc27A) (Lee et al., 2013) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing arsenite resistance of Fps13A in hog1Δ cells.

claim: Fps13A was still in the closed state in an Fps1 mutant (Fps1IVAA) that cannot bind Hog1.
source: We found, however, that Fps13A was still in the closed state, as judged by arsenite resistance, in the total absence of Hog1 (hog1Δ) (Figure 3A), or in an Fps1 mutant (Fps1IVAA) that cannot bind Hog1 or where the activator cannot be displaced from Fps1 by Hog1 phosphorylation (Rgc27A) (Lee et al., 2013) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing arsenite resistance of Fps1(3A)IVAA.

claim: Fps13A was still in the closed state where the activator cannot be displaced from Fps1 by Hog1 phosphorylation (Rgc27A).
source: We found, however, that Fps13A was still in the closed state, as judged by arsenite resistance, in the total absence of Hog1 (hog1Δ) (Figure 3A), or in an Fps1 mutant (Fps1IVAA) that cannot bind Hog1 or where the activator cannot be displaced from Fps1 by Hog1 phosphorylation (Rgc27A) (Lee et al., 2013) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing arsenite resistance of Fps13A in Rgc27A background.

claim: Closure of the Fps1 channel by lack of Ypk1 phosphorylation occurs independently of any effects requiring Hog1.
source: Thus, closure of the Fps1 channel by lack of Ypk1 phosphorylation occurs independently of any effects requiring Hog1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing Fps13A remains closed in hog1Δ and Hog1-insensitive mutant backgrounds.

claim: Presence or absence of Ypk1-mediated Fps1 phosphorylation had no effect on Fps1-Rgc2 interaction.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, presence or absence of Ypk1-mediated Fps1 phosphorylation had no effect on Fps1-Rgc2 interaction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Fps13A hog1Δ cells are significantly more resistant to hyperosmotic stress than otherwise isogenic hog1Δ cells.
source: Indeed, Fps13A hog1Δ cells are significantly more resistant to hyperosmotic stress than otherwise isogenic hog1Δ cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing growth of Fps13A hog1Δ cells on sorbitol plates.

claim: Even when Hog1 is absent, loss of Ypk1-mediated Fps1 channel opening is sufficient for cells to accumulate an adequate amount of glycerol to physiologically cope with hyperosmotic stress.
source: This epistasis confirms that, even when Hog1 is absent, loss of Ypk1-mediated Fps1 channel opening is sufficient for cells to accumulate an adequate amount of glycerol to physiologically cope with hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis experiment showing Fps13A suppresses hog1Δ hyperosmotic sensitivity.

claim: TORC2-dependent Ypk1-catalyzed phosphorylation of Fps1 opens this channel.
source: Aside from further validating the utility of our screen for identifying new Ypk1 substrates (Muir et al., 2014), our current findings demonstrate that TORC2-dependent Ypk1-catalyzed phosphorylation of Fps1 opens this channel and, conversely, that loss of Ypk1-dependent Fps1 phosphorylation upon hypertonic shock is sufficient to close the channel, prevent glycerol efflux, and promote cell survival.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Ypk1-dependent Fps1 phosphorylation upon hypertonic shock is sufficient to close the channel, prevent glycerol efflux, and promote cell survival.
source: Aside from further validating the utility of our screen for identifying new Ypk1 substrates (Muir et al., 2014), our current findings demonstrate that TORC2-dependent Ypk1-catalyzed phosphorylation of Fps1 opens this channel and, conversely, that loss of Ypk1-dependent Fps1 phosphorylation upon hypertonic shock is sufficient to close the channel, prevent glycerol efflux, and promote cell survival.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In a detailed kinetic analysis of global changes in the S. cerevisiae phosphoproteome upon hyperosmotic stress, two sites in Fps1 (S181 and T185) become dephosphorylated.
source: In agreement with our observations, in a detailed kinetic analysis of global changes in the S. cerevisiae phosphoproteome upon hyperosmotic stress (Kanshin et al., 2015), it was noted that two sites in Fps1 (S181 and T185), which we showed here are modified by Ypk1, become dephosphorylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kanshin et al., 2015.

claim: Gpd1 is the rate-limiting enzyme for glycerol production under hyperosmotic conditions.
source: We previously showed that Gpd1, the rate-limiting enzyme for glycerol production under hyperosmotic conditions (Remize et al., 2001), is negatively regulated by Ypk1 phosphorylation (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Remize et al., 2001.

claim: Gpd1 is negatively regulated by Ypk1 phosphorylation.
source: We previously showed that Gpd1, the rate-limiting enzyme for glycerol production under hyperosmotic conditions (Remize et al., 2001), is negatively regulated by Ypk1 phosphorylation (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: Inactivation of TORC2-Ypk1 signaling upon hyperosmotic shock has at least two coordinated consequences that work synergistically to cause glycerol accumulation and promote cell survival.
source: Thus, inactivation of TORC2-Ypk1 signaling upon hyperosmotic shock has at least two coordinated consequences that work synergistically to cause glycerol accumulation and promote cell survival, a similar outcome but mechanistically distinct from the processes evoked by Hog1 activation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating the findings about Gpd1 and Fps1 regulation.

claim: Loss of TORC2-Ypk1 signaling alleviates inhibition of Gpd1, which, combined with transcriptional induction of GPD1 by hyperosmotic stress, greatly increases glycerol production.
source: First, loss of TORC2-Ypk1 signaling alleviates inhibition of Gpd1, which, combined with transcriptional induction of GPD1 by hyperosmotic stress, greatly increases glycerol production.
evidence: This is inferred from the known regulation of Gpd1 by Ypk1 and transcriptional induction of GPD1.

claim: Loss of TORC2-Ypk1 signaling closes the Fps1 channel, thereby retaining the glycerol produced.
source: Second, loss of TORC2-Ypk1 signaling closes the Fps1 channel, thereby retaining the glycerol produced.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing Fps1 closure upon loss of Ypk1 phosphorylation.

claim: Presence of two systems (TORC2-Ypk1 and Hog1) might allow cells to adjust optimally to stresses occurring with different intensity, duration, or frequency.
source: Presence of two systems (TORC2-Ypk1 and Hog1) might allow cells to adjust optimally to stresses occurring with different intensity, duration, or frequency.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential advantage of having two parallel systems.

claim: Hog1 responds to stresses occurring no more frequently than every 200 s.
source: Reportedly, Hog1 responds to stresses occurring no more frequently than every 200 s (Hersen et al., 2008; McClean et al., 2009), whereas we found TORC2-Ypk1 signaling responded to hypertonic stress in ≤60 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hersen et al., 2008 and McClean et al., 2009.

claim: TORC2-Ypk1 signaling responded to hypertonic stress in ≤60 s.
source: Reportedly, Hog1 responds to stresses occurring no more frequently than every 200 s (Hersen et al., 2008; McClean et al., 2009), whereas we found TORC2-Ypk1 signaling responded to hypertonic stress in ≤60 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rapid Ypk1 dephosphorylation within 1 min.

claim: The Sln1 and Sho1 sensors that lead to Hog1 activation likely can respond to stimuli that do not affect the TORC2-Ypk1 axis, and vice-versa.
source: Also, the Sln1 and Sho1 sensors that lead to Hog1 activation likely can respond to stimuli that do not affect the TORC2-Ypk1 axis, and vice-versa.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential differential responsiveness of the two pathways.

claim: Rapid and profound reduction in phosphorylation of Ypk1 at its TORC2 sites upon hyperosmotic stress could arise from activation of a phosphatase (other than CN), inhibition of TORC2 catalytic activity, or both.
source: A remaining question is how hyperosmotic stress causes such a rapid and profound reduction in phosphorylation of Ypk1 at its TORC2 sites. This outcome could arise from activation of a phosphatase (other than CN), inhibition of TORC2 catalytic activity, or both.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: A recent report showed that Tor2 (the catalytic component of TORC2) interacts physically with Sho1.
source: Despite a recent report that Tor2 (the catalytic component of TORC2) interacts physically with Sho1 (Lam et al., 2015), raising the possibility that a Hog1 pathway sensor directly modulates TORC2 activity, we found that hyperosmolarity inactivates TORC2 just as robustly in sho1Δ cells as in wild-type cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lam et al., 2015.

claim: Hyperosmolarity inactivates TORC2 just as robustly in sho1Δ cells as in wild-type cells.
source: Despite a recent report that Tor2 (the catalytic component of TORC2) interacts physically with Sho1 (Lam et al., 2015), raising the possibility that a Hog1 pathway sensor directly modulates TORC2 activity, we found that hyperosmolarity inactivates TORC2 just as robustly in sho1Δ cells as in wild-type cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Ypk1 dephosphorylation in sho1Δ cells.

claim: The ancillary TORC2 subunits Slm1 and Slm2 play a role in delivering Ypk1 to the TORC2 complex.
source: Alternatively, given the role ascribed to the ancillary TORC2 subunits Slm1 and Slm2 (Gaubitz et al., 2015) in delivering Ypk1 to the TORC2 complex (Berchtold et al., 2012; Niles et al., 2012), response to hyperosmotic shock might be mediated by some influence on Slm1 and Slm2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berchtold et al., 2012 and Niles et al., 2012.

claim: Response to hyperosmotic shock might be mediated by some influence on Slm1 and Slm2.
source: Alternatively, given the role ascribed to the ancillary TORC2 subunits Slm1 and Slm2 (Gaubitz et al., 2015) in delivering Ypk1 to the TORC2 complex (Berchtold et al., 2012; Niles et al., 2012), response to hyperosmotic shock might be mediated by some influence on Slm1 and Slm2.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: The down-regulation of TORC2-Ypk1 signaling and its consequences represent a novel mechanism for sensing and responding to hyperosmolarity.
source: Thus, although the mechanism that abrogates TORC2 phosphorylation of Ypk1 upon hypertonic stress remains to be delineated, this effect and its consequences represent a novel mechanism for sensing and responding to hyperosmolarity.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding of the manuscript.
